paragraphs: Discrete flow matching generates discrete outputs through a process of changes over continuous time. Running that process requires numerical sampling, and quality can suffer when only a small number of model evaluations is affordable. TR-CIE changes how the sampler advances through time and estimates the accumulated intensity of transitions within each step.

Its first component reshapes the time grid according to the noise schedule. Under standard factorized rate parameterizations, this absorbs a schedule-dependent growth term and reduces numerical stiffness near the end of sampling. Its second component reuses model outputs cached from the previous step to improve estimates of cumulative transition intensities on the resulting uneven grid.

The authors bound local approximation error and establish convergence results. Each step still needs only one model evaluation, matching the evaluation count of standard tau-leaping. Experiments on synthetic tasks, text generation, and text-to-image generation report better sampling quality with limited evaluations. The contribution is therefore a way to extract more sampling accuracy from the same evaluation budget.
icml-2026-a-time-reparameterized-cumulat.tldr: TR-CIE improves discrete flow sampling under limited model evaluations by reshaping sampling time and reusing previous model outputs.

paragraphs: A coding agent can produce a strong first solution yet struggle to improve it after testing. CATArena evaluates this distinction through repeated tournaments, extending assessment beyond whether an agent generates functional code in a single attempt. Its central question is how effectively an agent develops its code over multiple rounds.

During tournaments, agents receive execution feedback and refine their programs using both reflection on their own work and learning from peers. A dual-metric evaluation separates initial code-generation proficiency from the ability to improve. This makes development over time a distinct object of measurement, rather than allowing the quality of the first submission to stand in for iterative capability.

The experiments find that initial proficiency does not strictly track improvement potential. They also show that current agents have difficulty benefiting from peer-learning and self-reflection simultaneously. The authors report evidence of extensibility and robustness across task variation. Together, these findings support evaluating code agents through their response to feedback as well as through their initial output.
icml-2026-catarena-evaluating-evolutiona.tldr: CATArena uses iterative coding tournaments to distinguish agents’ initial coding ability from their capacity to improve through feedback.

paragraphs: Camouflaged object detection requires predicting which image pixels belong to an object that blends into its surroundings. Diffusion approaches can refine these predicted masks over several sampling steps. CODiff reformulates the process to produce a mask in one step, aiming to retain strong detection accuracy while removing repeated sampling.

The paper first establishes theoretical feasibility for one-step sampling in this task. It then designs a network specifically for that setting. Global semantic guidance helps direct denoising using overall image meaning, while hierarchical condition integration supplies finer structural information. An additional regularizer improves intermediate features by reducing the representation gap between the conditioning backbone and the diffusion model.

Experiments report state-of-the-art performance across multiple benchmarks, including an improvement of more than 22% in mean absolute error on COD10K. These findings show that, in the evaluated setting, one-step prediction can support strong mask accuracy. The architectural components explain how CODiff supplies both broad semantic guidance and detailed structure within that single inference step.
icml-2026-codiff-one-step-diffusion-mode.tldr: CODiff predicts camouflaged-object masks in one diffusion step and reports state-of-the-art accuracy across multiple benchmarks.

paragraphs: Slice sampling is widely used to draw posterior samples from Dirichlet process models, but its computational demands are difficult to characterize. The amount of work in an iteration is random and can, in principle, be unbounded. This paper develops probability-based complexity guarantees to explain how that cost scales.

The central result concerns extra work introduced by slice variables relative to the number of clusters supported by the posterior. Across different posterior cluster-growth regimes, this overhead is logarithmic in the dataset size in a probabilistic sense. The result controls the likelihood of large costs; it does not impose a fixed deterministic ceiling on every iteration.

The analysis implies that superlinear per-iteration cost blow-ups become vanishingly unlikely, even in worst-case configurations. It applies broadly to Dirichlet process models without assumptions tailored to a particular likelihood, and provides guarantees for arbitrary datasets. This supplies a theoretical basis for judging practical scalability despite the sampler’s potentially unbounded iteration cost.
icml-2026-complexity-bounds-for-dirichle.tldr: The paper gives probabilistic complexity bounds showing that excessive per-iteration costs become unlikely for Dirichlet process slice samplers.

paragraphs: Instruction-tuning data can be problematic for different reasons: an example may repeat information already present, or it may contain a quality defect. Cure-SFT treats these as separate curation problems. Its goal is to improve instruction-following training while balancing quality, diversity, and consistency with the data distribution.

The method works from coarse selection to finer diagnosis. It first removes redundant examples through stratified sampling based on semantic and geometric structure. Teacher models then diagnose the remaining examples, and targeted remediation repairs samples with fixable defects. This sequence gives redundancy reduction and quality repair distinct roles, rather than treating every undesirable example as a candidate for the same intervention.

In the reported experiments, Cure-SFT can exceed the performance of instruction tuning on the full dataset while using only 10% of the data budget. It also consistently outperforms strong selection and rewriting baselines across budgets. These findings support the value of diagnosing what is wrong with an example before deciding how to curate it.
icml-2026-cure-sft-diagnostic-guided-dat.tldr: Cure-SFT separates redundant instructions from defective ones, enabling targeted curation that can outperform full-data tuning with 10% of the data budget.

paragraphs: Personalized image generation becomes harder when several reference concepts must appear together while retaining their distinctive appearance. This paper addresses that challenge by separating composition into structure alignment and texture rendering. Its Sketch-to-Rendering framework uses optimal transport in both stages to coordinate where visual information goes.

The structure stage uses mass-preserving transport to align shapes and maintain spatial consistency. The texture stage follows that established geometry: low-frequency structural alignment guides the transfer of high-frequency detail through transport-based residuals. This division gives overall arrangement and fine appearance separate treatments, with texture injection designed to preserve the structure established earlier.

Experiments report significant improvements in fidelity to the reference concepts and in visual quality. Ablation studies also support the contribution of optimal transport guidance and the decision to separate structure from texture. The findings suggest that organizing these two demands explicitly can improve multi-concept generation, where transferring appearance and maintaining coherent shapes must work together.
icml-2026-dual-optimal-transport-for-mul.tldr: The framework uses separate optimal transport stages to align reference-concept shapes and add texture while preserving structure.

paragraphs: Diffusion language models can generate tokens in parallel, but training them from scratch is less learning-efficient than training autoregressive models. Efficient-DLM studies how to convert pretrained autoregressive models into diffusion models while retaining task accuracy and gaining generation speed. It focuses on attention structure and the masking patterns used during training.

The authors find that preserving pretrained weight distributions is important for effective conversion. Their continued pretraining scheme uses block-wise attention, whose causal structure better preserves those distributions while also enabling KV caching. A second change gives later token positions higher masking probabilities, bringing training masks closer to the strongly left-to-right patterns encountered at test time.

The resulting model family improves reported accuracy–throughput trade-offs against state-of-the-art autoregressive and diffusion models. Efficient-DLM-8B reports 5.4% and 2.7% higher accuracy, with 4.7-fold and 2.8-fold higher throughput, relative to Dream-7B and Qwen3-4B respectively. These results support adapting both attention and training masks when transferring pretrained autoregressive capabilities into parallel generation.
icml-2026-efficient-dlm-from-autoregress.tldr: Efficient-DLM converts pretrained autoregressive models into fast diffusion models using block-wise attention and position-dependent training masks.

paragraphs: An agent’s observations, environment dynamics, and objectives can all change, while rewards may arrive sparsely or late. FlowMAP addresses planning under this shifting mixture by representing planning as a continuous transformation of a meta-state distribution. A learned velocity field moves that distribution toward a target conditioned on the task.

Its Value-Transport Flow Matching objective guides this movement toward regions with high value. Working at the distribution level is intended to reduce accumulated planning error under environmental shifts. A second component, Flow–Policy Co-Training, jointly trains the planning flow and the action policy so that the planned transformation regularizes the distribution changes produced by actual agent–environment interaction.

This coupling matters because a planning distribution needs to remain connected to what the policy can accomplish through actions. Across diverse planning benchmarks, FlowMAP consistently outperforms strong baselines and improves generalization. The results support the proposed combination of value-directed distribution transport and joint policy training as an approach to planning in changing environments.
icml-2026-flowmap-flow-matching-for-gene.tldr: FlowMAP jointly trains a planning flow and action policy to move state distributions toward high-value outcomes under environmental shifts.

paragraphs: Diffusion language models can fill multiple token positions in parallel, yet choosing only highly confident predictions can restrict progress. This paper analyzes that restriction through an information-theoretic lower bound. The required decoding rounds grow with the sample’s total information and shrink as the amount of information obtainable per round increases.

The proposed Explore-Then-Exploit strategy uses this observation to change decoding without additional training. It combines decoding across blocks with targeted exploration of uncertain tokens. Resolving selected uncertain positions can reshape the conditional distribution and make other positions easier to predict, triggering cascades of confident token decisions.

Experiments across diverse benchmarks support the theoretical bounds and show fewer decoding rounds than confidence-only baselines without compromising generation quality. The method also works efficiently with KV caching, turning the reduction in rounds into higher tokens-per-second throughput. Its contribution is to treat uncertainty as something the decoder can selectively explore to unlock progress, rather than relying exclusively on positions that are already easy to predict.
icml-2026-from-bits-to-rounds-parallel-d.tldr: Explore-Then-Exploit speeds diffusion language decoding by resolving selected uncertain tokens that unlock further confident predictions.

paragraphs: A multimodal agent may perform well after fine-tuning yet struggle with unfamiliar applications, changed interfaces, or workflows spanning several apps. This paper argues that a key bottleneck is whether the agent has enough procedural knowledge: knowledge of the steps needed to accomplish the requested goal.

The proposed Procedure-Aware Multimodal Agent with Meta Reasoning represents that knowledge explicitly as natural-language procedures. A grounded agent is trained to choose actions conditioned on these procedures. Procedural knowledge can come from a language model’s general capabilities or, when necessary, external resources such as web search. The framework therefore gives task instructions an explicit role in connecting knowledge to interface actions.

The authors report substantial improvements on challenging Android benchmarks, with generalization across tasks, applications, interface versions, and multi-app workflows. These findings support training agents to use procedural knowledge from different sources. The practical significance is that adapting behavior can depend on obtaining and applying the relevant procedure, alongside the agent’s learned ability to act.
icml-2026-hierarchical-procedural-meta-r.tldr: The framework improves multimodal agent generalization by conditioning actions on explicit natural-language procedures drawn from internal or external knowledge.

paragraphs: Sharing network parameters makes multi-agent reinforcement learning more efficient, but agents can push the same weights toward conflicting updates. HPS analyzes those updates geometrically, separating changes to a weight vector’s direction from changes to its magnitude. The authors find that agents largely agree on directional changes while disagreeing substantially on scale.

That finding motivates sharing directions while allowing agent-specific scales. HPS constrains the shared backbone weights to a unit hypersphere, so shared learning changes their direction. A separate scale generator supplies multiplicative factors for each agent. This lets agents express different response magnitudes while retaining the directional learning they have in common.

The paper argues that splitting a shared network into agent-specific subnetworks can lose useful shared directional updates along with the conflicts. HPS instead targets the identified scale conflict directly. Experiments on SMAC, SMACv2, VMAS, and Predator Prey report significant gains over state-of-the-art methods, supporting this separation as an effective way to combine parameter sharing with behavioral diversity.
icml-2026-hps-hyperspherical-parameter-s.tldr: HPS shares weight directions across agents while learning individual scales to reduce gradient conflict without discarding common learning.

paragraphs: Climate time series reflect both hidden driving processes and direct influences among observed variables. Methods focused only on latent factors can overlook the latter relationships. This paper develops a unified framework for recovering observed-variable causal links together with latent drivers and their interactions.

The theoretical contribution identifies conditions under which both parts can be recovered simultaneously from time-series data. These guarantees extend to a nonparametric setting and use contextual information to recover hidden variables and observable relationships. Guided by that analysis, the authors introduce CaDRe, a generative time-series model whose structural constraints combine causal representation learning with causal discovery.

Synthetic experiments validate the theoretical results. On real climate datasets, CaDRe achieves competitive forecasting accuracy and produces visualized causal graphs that align with domain expertise. That agreement provides interpretable climate insights, while the formal recovery claim remains conditional on the established identifiability requirements. The contribution is a framework that models hidden drivers and direct observed influences together rather than leaving one part outside the analysis.
icml-2026-learning-general-causal-struct.tldr: CaDRe jointly models hidden climate drivers and causal links among observed variables, with conditional identifiability guarantees and interpretable empirical results.

paragraphs: Neural models of physical dynamics can incorporate conservation laws to make their predictions physically plausible. Scaling such models to high-dimensional systems remains difficult. The Reduced-order Hamiltonian Neural Network, or RO-HNN, addresses this by combining Hamiltonian mechanics with a learned lower-dimensional description of the system.

Its first component is a geometrically constrained symplectic autoencoder. This learns a lower-dimensional submanifold while preserving the geometric structure needed for Hamiltonian dynamics. Its second component is a geometric Hamiltonian neural network that learns motion on that submanifold. The two components connect compression and dynamics modeling through a shared physical structure.

This connection matters because the reduced representation is designed to retain structure relevant to the conservation laws used by the dynamics model. Experiments report physically consistent, stable predictions that generalize across complex high-dimensional dynamics. The findings support model order reduction as a way to extend Hamiltonian neural networks to larger physical systems while retaining the benefits of incorporating physical principles into the architecture.
icml-2026-learning-hamiltonian-dynamics-.tldr: RO-HNN learns a compact, structure-preserving representation of physical systems and models Hamiltonian dynamics within it.

paragraphs: Updating a multimodal model involves two distinct situations: teaching it something previously unknown and replacing something it learned correctly before the world changed. MMKU-Bench evaluates both. It also addresses cross-modal consistency, extending evaluation beyond whether updated knowledge works within the same modality in which it was assessed.

The benchmark contains more than 25,000 knowledge instances and over 49,000 images. Its two knowledge scenarios enable comparisons between learning new information and revising established knowledge. The authors use it to evaluate supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning from human feedback, and knowledge editing, bringing these approaches into a common evaluation framework.

The experiments reveal different weaknesses. Supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning from human feedback are prone to catastrophic forgetting, meaning updates can undermine previously learned capabilities. Knowledge editing better preserves general capabilities but has clear limitations when updates continue over time. These findings make the benchmark useful for examining both successful knowledge change and the ability to sustain broader model competence through repeated updating.
icml-2026-mmku-bench-a-multimodal-update.tldr: MMKU-Bench evaluates learning new and changed multimodal knowledge, revealing forgetting and continual-update weaknesses in representative methods.

paragraphs: Multimodal models can learn relational tasks from a few demonstrations, but the internal representations enabling that behavior are difficult to identify. This paper finds that a small subset of attention heads transmits visual-relation representations. The authors extract activations from these heads as function vectors that can be manipulated during inference.

Using synthetic and real images, they apply causal mediation analysis to identify heads that strongly influence relational predictions. Extracted vectors improve zero-shot accuracy. The vectors can also be fine-tuned with a modest amount of data while the underlying model parameters remain frozen, significantly outperforming the evaluated in-context learning baselines.

The authors further show that linear combinations of relation-specific vectors can solve analogy problems involving visual relations absent from training. Experiments on OpenFlamingo and Qwen3-VL support the presence of localized, adjustable structures carrying relational knowledge. These results connect an interpretability finding to a practical intervention: extracting and optimizing internal activations can improve control over relational reasoning without updating the full model.
icml-2026-multimodal-function-vectors-fo.tldr: Visual-relation function vectors extracted from selected attention heads improve relational predictions and can combine to solve novel analogies.

paragraphs: Multiview subspace clustering seeks underlying groups in high-dimensional data described through multiple views. The paper identifies two difficulties in existing approaches: conventional convex low-rank approximations can miss higher-order relationships across views, and methods struggle to retain global correlations together with local geometric patterns. Noise and outliers further weaken clustering.

The proposed model combines nonconvex low-rank regularization with a deep prior. The low-rank component is designed to characterize shared underlying structure and suppress outlier effects, while deep networks preserve local structural properties. Combining them gives the model separate mechanisms for capturing broad cross-view relationships and finer patterns within the data.

The authors analyze the optimization problem’s optimal solution and derive an efficient algorithm based on ADMM, with provable convergence guarantees. Experiments across multiple datasets report superior clustering performance. The contribution therefore includes both a richer representation objective and a supported procedure for solving it. The empirical results back the proposed combination of global low-rank structure, outlier handling, and learned local information.
icml-2026-nonconvex-low-rank-tensor-repr.tldr: The method combines nonconvex low-rank modeling and deep priors to improve multiview clustering while preserving global and local structure.

paragraphs: Human preferences provide a basis for comparing language models, but turning those comparisons into reliable rankings poses statistical challenges. Restrictive ranking models can limit flexibility, while flexible machine learning methods can complicate uncertainty quantification. DMLRank introduces a nonparametric framework based on debiased machine learning to address these problems together.

The framework defines generalized average ranking scores, which extend familiar approaches including Bradley–Terry and PageRank or Rank centrality. These scores accommodate richer preference responses such as ties. DMLRank provides statistically efficient score estimates and allows black-box machine learning methods to participate in estimation, making flexible prediction compatible with its statistical ranking framework.

It can also incorporate pretrained language-model evaluators and suggests optimal strategies for gathering preference data under a limited budget. The authors support these advantages through theory and experiments on synthetic and real preference datasets. The contribution links ranking, uncertainty, and data collection: practitioners can use expressive estimation tools while assessing model comparisons and deciding how to spend their evaluation budget.
icml-2026-nonparametric-llm-evaluation-f.tldr: DMLRank combines flexible preference modeling with statistically grounded ranking estimates and budget-aware preference collection.

paragraphs: Matching a whole image to a sentence does not necessarily provide precise matches between individual objects and phrases. ObjEmbed addresses this finer-grained problem by producing regional representations for individual objects alongside a representation of the full image. The same model supports visual grounding and both local and global image retrieval.

Each region receives two complementary embeddings. An object embedding captures semantic information for matching descriptions, while an IoU embedding predicts localization quality. The final matching score combines semantic similarity with that predicted quality. This allows retrieval to account for both what a region depicts and how well it is localized.

ObjEmbed encodes all objects and the full image in a single forward pass, supporting efficiency across its regional and global uses. Results on 18 benchmarks report superior performance and strong semantic discrimination. The contribution is a unified representation that connects object meaning with spatial quality, allowing fine-grained matching and whole-image retrieval to share an encoding process.
icml-2026-objembed-towards-universal-mul.tldr: ObjEmbed encodes objects and whole images together, combining semantic similarity with predicted localization quality for more accurate matching.

paragraphs: Few-step diffusion reduces repeated model evaluations, but large full-precision networks still demand substantial resources. Q-Sched addresses the remaining burden through post-training quantization at the scheduler level. It keeps quantized weights fixed and adjusts sampling coefficients to account for quantization along the generation trajectory.

Those coefficients are learned with a Joint Alignment–Quality loss combining text–image compatibility and image quality. Calibration uses only a handful of prompts and requires no full-precision inference. The method reports a fourfold model-size reduction while retaining a reusable checkpoint across bit-widths, with generation quality matching or exceeding full precision in the evaluated settings.

Reported FID improvements are 15.5% over a full-precision four-step Latent Consistency Model and 16.6% over a full-precision eight-step Phased Consistency Model. A user study exceeding 80,000 annotations further supports results on FLUX.1[schnell] and SDXL-Turbo. These findings show that adapting the sampler can help quantization and few-step generation work together, rather than treating reduced weight precision as a change the sampling process must simply tolerate.
icml-2026-q-sched-pushing-the-boundaries.tldr: Q-Sched adapts diffusion sampling to fixed quantized weights, reporting smaller models and improved quality without full-precision calibration.

paragraphs: Combining language models can improve performance, but explicitly averaging their next-token distributions requires running every participating model. Mixture-model-like Ensemble, or ME, reinterprets that average as a mixture distribution. This perspective changes how a token can be sampled without first calculating the complete ensemble distribution.

At each generation step, ME randomly selects one model and uses it to generate the next token. The paper establishes that this procedure is mathematically equivalent to sampling from the ensemble distribution. The equivalence concerns sampling: the method reproduces the mixture’s sampling behavior while invoking only one model for that step.

The authors report speedups of 1.78 to 2.68 times over conventional ensembling. They also connect this formulation to token-level routing, where a choice determines which model handles a token, suggesting that ensembling is a special case of routing. The result provides both an efficient implementation and a conceptual link between combining model predictions and selecting models during generation.
icml-2026-rethinking-llm-ensembling-from.tldr: ME samples from an ensemble distribution by randomly invoking one model per token, yielding reported speedups of 1.78–2.68 times.

paragraphs: Researchers sometimes infer language-model features from singular vectors of attention matrices, but the reason this works has lacked a firm explanation. This paper asks when those mathematical directions align with meaningful feature representations and how such alignment might be detected when the features themselves cannot be observed directly.

The authors first demonstrate robust alignment in a model where features are directly observable. They then establish theoretically that alignment is expected under a range of conditions. This connects an empirical observation to conditions that can justify using singular vectors as clues to a model’s internal representations.

For real models, the paper identifies sparse attention decomposition as a testable prediction of alignment. The authors find evidence that this decomposition appears in a way consistent with their predictions. Together, the controlled demonstration, theory, and real-model evidence suggest that singular vectors can provide a sound basis for feature identification. The conclusion supports this approach under relevant conditions rather than asserting that every singular vector always corresponds to a feature.
icml-2026-singular-vectors-of-attention-.tldr: The paper provides theoretical and empirical support for identifying model features through singular vectors of attention matrices under relevant conditions.

paragraphs: Many reasoning problems retain their structure when symbols or colors are renamed consistently. Existing recurrent reasoning models learn to handle these changes implicitly through costly data augmentation. Symbol-Equivariant Recurrent Reasoning Models build the symmetry directly into their layers, so consistently permuting input symbols produces correspondingly permuted solutions.

This architectural guarantee removes the need to learn that particular consistency solely from examples. On Sudoku, the proposed models outperform prior recurrent reasoning models on 9-by-9 puzzles. After training only on that size, they also generalize to 4-by-4, 16-by-16, and 25-by-25 instances, sizes to which the existing models in the study cannot extrapolate.

On ARC-AGI-1 and ARC-AGI-2, the models achieve competitive performance with substantially less augmentation and only two million parameters. These findings support explicitly encoding symbol symmetry as a useful design choice for compact reasoning systems. The symmetry guarantee concerns consistency under relabeling; the broader gains in puzzle performance and size generalization are empirical results.
icml-2026-symbol-equivariant-recurrent-r.tldr: Symbol-equivariant layers improve recurrent reasoning models’ robustness to relabeling and support strong empirical generalization across Sudoku sizes.

paragraphs: A robot can estimate its chance of completing a task at many points during execution, although success is known only at the end. This paper formalizes calibration for that sequential setting, including the challenge of observing only partial trajectories. The aim is to make confidence along an episode meaningfully reflect eventual task success.

The authors extend the Brier score to sequential tasks and show that, for binary outcomes, the quantity minimizing its risk equals the vision-language-action policy’s value function. This connects uncertainty calibration to reinforcement learning: temporal-difference value estimation becomes a principled way to adjust success confidence as the episode unfolds.

Experiments on simulated and real-robot data show improved performance relative to state-of-the-art calibration approaches. The authors also find that single-step action probabilities can provide competitive uncertainty estimates after temporal-difference calibration. That result differs from findings using other calibration techniques and suggests that the usefulness of these probabilities depends partly on how they are calibrated over time.
icml-2026-temporal-difference-calibratio.tldr: Temporal-difference calibration links a robot’s evolving success confidence to value estimation and improves reported uncertainty performance.

paragraphs: Conditional independence asks whether two variables remain related after accounting for other variables. It is central to causal analysis and feature selection, but testing it requires additional assumptions in many settings. This paper investigates whether learned representations can improve the adaptability and scalability of principled kernel-based tests.

The method builds representations from the singular value decomposition of partial covariance operators and uses them in a simple test statistic. A bi-level contrastive algorithm learns those representations. This connects a mathematically motivated description of conditional relationships with a representation-learning procedure intended to make the approach more practical.

The theory relates representation-learning error to test performance and establishes asymptotic validity and power guarantees. These concern behavior as sample size grows, including the ability to control erroneous findings and detect dependence. Experiments on synthetic and real data suggest a statistically grounded path toward scalable testing. The contribution preserves the connection between learned representations and statistical guarantees while addressing limitations of existing kernel approaches.
icml-2026-toward-scalable-and-valid-cond.tldr: The paper learns spectral representations for conditional independence testing and links their accuracy to asymptotic statistical guarantees.

paragraphs: Time-series foundation models often emphasize forecasting without additional training, while other analysis tasks still require specialized tuning. Zeus aims to support a broader set of tasks without task-specific fine-tuning. It addresses both the cost of processing long sequences and the different kinds of temporal information that different tasks require.

Its architecture uses point-wise tokenization within a multi-scale Transformer organized as a U-shaped hierarchy. This combines fine-grained representation with long-sequence efficiency. Its Multi-Objective Temporal Masking strategy supports tasks requiring different biases, including extrapolation, interpolation, and global abstraction, within one framework. Together, these choices address representation scale and task diversity.

Across five representative tasks, experiments report consistently competitive results in tuning-free settings. These findings support the potential of a shared time-series model whose usefulness extends beyond forecasting without requiring separate adaptation for every task. The contribution is the combination of a scalable architecture and a unified masking strategy designed to make that broader generalization possible.
icml-2026-zeus-towards-tuning-free-found.tldr: Zeus combines multi-scale processing and multi-objective temporal masking to support diverse time-series tasks without task-specific fine-tuning.
